title: READ THE F*CKING STICKY - The Best Lifting Advice on 4chan /fit/ (Myths & Mindset)
summary: NH reviews the 4chan /fit/ sticky, the board's long-standing beginner document, section by section. He agrees with its myth-busting on women getting bulky, lifting being confusing and spot reduction, plus its mindset advice on lifelong habits and incremental change, but rejects its claim that abs are made in the kitchen and its heavy low-rep ab advice.
claims: Old 4chan /fit/ shaped much of his advice because it was a place where nobody tried to sell you anything; today the board itself is garbage but the free sticky remains a good document
Lifting cannot make women bulky like men because they lack the characteristics to blow up; it rounds the glutes, shapes the quads and arms and makes women look more feminine
Old bodybuilding magazines were around 90% wrong and told women to avoid heavy weights, producing a generation who thought yoga and occasional jogging were enough
Women need muscle mass to stay healthy and mobile just as much as men

He disagrees that women should train exactly like men: a woman uninterested in upper-body size gains nothing from training it three times a week and may not recover from it; programs should be tailored to women
Only about 2% of his viewers are female, but he may write a women-specific program
Confusion in fitness comes from the people presenting information, not the information: YouTube cliques and gurus push their ideology as the only thing that works
Almost everything works for a novice; only as you advance do you need a more specific approach
The people most confused by contradictory advice are those who never actually lift; training yourself builds critical thinking about principles
Most fitness contradictions are hair-splitting; volume arguments between influencers are about ego, since every individual needs different volume and frequency
Influencers invent gimmicks and new variables to sell products they receive from sponsors
Lifting is simple, especially at the start; you don't need a PhD, and only about 10% of the value is knowledge while 90% is applying it
Spot reduction is a myth: fat comes off all over through a calorie deficit or a recomposition
Recomposition beats pure fat loss: it helps prevent stretch marks and loose skin, and more muscle raises the calories you can eat at maintenance
Fat-loss creams rubbed on the abs are snake oil aimed at lazy people
You can make a fatty area look better by training it: bigger muscle spreads the fat over a larger area and vascularity makes it look leaner
There is some evidence that long, high-rep sets cause slightly more local fat loss, but the effect is tiny (about 1 versus 100 for diet), so a million crunches won't fix a fat belly
Men left with fatty chest tissue after weight loss can improve it a little by growing the pecs and training them for the pump
Abs are not made in the kitchen: dieting only reveals them, and visible, three-dimensional abs that pop like bread rolls with gaps between them come from training
The sticky's advice to do abs heavy with a plate for 5-10 reps is a powerlifting mindset that won't build a six-pack
Train abs like calves: frequently, with high volume and moderate-to-low intensity; going heavy on abs does nothing
Abs grow under fat just like other muscles, so training them during a bulk and cutting later can reveal well-developed abs
Claims that ab exercises don't change how you look reflect the writer's own frustration; influencers' statements are biased by their experience
Lifting is a lifelong pursuit: whatever you gain with work you must keep with work
About 70% of people cycle through six months of training, mediocre results and quitting, which never produces anything great
People who start extreme (cutting 2000 kcal, training twice a day) burn out, often subconsciously on purpose so they can say it was too hard
Training like a normal person for two years is far more work and far more effective than training like a madman for two weeks; change must be incremental
Beginners stay hooked through results, like getting paid for work; later you train for mental stability and habit
The David Goggins effect: people copy an extreme figure on day one, fail and then resent self-improvement; start where you can touch the bottom
Training should be scheduled like lunch so there is never a question of whether you will train
Bad habits start pleasurable and become painful; good habits start painful and become pleasurable, so trust reason over sensation
The wrong thing done consistently beats the right thing done sparingly: a kid doing daily chin-ups and push-ups at the park beats someone running a perfect paid program every two weeks
Most /fit/ posters have never read the sticky and lack the mindset it preaches
exercises: NH rejects it; abs need high volume, moderate load
consistency beats a perfect program done rarely
